meta.title: Who really said "The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Edmund Burke never wrote it. No source exists anywhere in his works; the closest documented line is John Stuart Mill's 1867 St Andrews address. Full evidence trail.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Burke. Bartlett's cited an 1795 letter that doesn't contain it, then retracted. The closest real source is John Stuart Mill, St Andrews, 1867, page 36.

answer.label: Not Edmund Burke — no such sentence exists in his works
answer.authorDates: Credited to Edmund Burke (1729–1797) · earliest known Burke credit, July 1920
answer.sourceLine: No one has ever located this sentence in Burke. Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations printed it under his name in 1968 and cited a specific document — his letter to William Smith of 9 January 1795 — but that letter contains nothing of the kind, and Bartlett’s fifteenth edition in 1980 acknowledged the line had not been located in his writings. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the earliest credit to Burke only as far back as a July 1920 church address, and concludes the record is too incomplete to say who actually crafted the wording.

source.heading: The closest documented source

docMeta.dd: Inaugural Address Delivered to the University of St. Andrews, Feb. 1st 1867
John Stuart Mill (1806–1873), Lord Rector of the University of St Andrews
1 February 1867 · printed London: Longmans, Green, Reader, and Dyer, 1867, p. 36
Antecedent only — the famous wording appears in no located source, by Mill or anyone else

source.excerpt: Let not any one pacify his conscience by the delusion that he can do no harm if he takes no part, and forms no opinion. Bad men need nothing more to compass their ends, than that good men should look on and do nothing.
source.trailTitle: How a sentence nobody wrote became Burke’s
trail: 1770 — the real Burke sentence, and it is not this one. Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ records, from Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770): “When bad men combine, the good must associate; else they will fall one by one, an unpitied sacrifice in a contemptible struggle.” Wikiquote notes this passage is often cited as the likely origin of the more famous line. It is related in spirit and nowhere near it in wording — and its subject is forming a political party, not standing idly by.

1867 — Mill states the idea plainly. On page 36 of his St Andrews inaugural address ↗, delivered 1 February 1867: “Bad men need nothing more to compass their ends, than that good men should look on and do nothing.” Closer than Burke, still not the sentence on the poster.

1916–1920 — the modern shape appears, then acquires a famous name. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the Rev. Charles F. Aked in the San Jose Mercury Herald of 31 October 1916: “For evil men to accomplish their purpose it is only necessary that good men should do nothing” — prefaced with “It has been said,” not claimed as his own. On 5 July 1920, at the Fourth International Congregational Council in Boston, Sir R. Murray Hyslop told his audience: “Burke once said: ‘The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men should do nothing.’” That is the earliest credit to Burke that QI has located.

1961–1980 — a president repeats it, a reference book retracts it. Quote Investigator ↗ documents President John F. Kennedy quoting the modern wording to the Canadian Parliament on 17 May 1961 and crediting Burke; Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations made it official in its 1968 fourteenth edition, citing Burke’s letter to William Smith of 9 January 1795. William Safire challenged the attribution in The New York Times in 1980 after it was confirmed the letter contained no such quote, and Bartlett’s fifteenth edition conceded the quotation had not been located in Burke’s writings.
source.excerptNote: This is Mill in 1867, not the sentence people quote. It is the nearest documented expression of the thought that anyone has produced from a primary source — but it is not the popular wording, and Mill did not write that wording either.

source.rightsNote: No copyright status can honestly be asserted for the famous sentence, because it has no traceable first publication and no identified author. The two documented texts quoted on this page are both long out of copyright — Burke’s Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (first published 23 April 1770) and Mill’s St Andrews inaugural address (1867) — but neither of them contains the wording people actually quote.

author.name: John Stuart Mill
author.heading: Who came nearest, and when
author.metaLine: 1806–1873 · English philosopher, economist & MP for Westminster
author.bio: John Stuart Mill was the leading English philosopher of liberalism in the nineteenth century, author of On Liberty and Utilitarianism, a career administrator for the East India Company, and Liberal MP for the City of Westminster from 1865 to 1868. Elected Lord Rector of the University of St Andrews, he used his inaugural address of 1 February 1867 to argue that private citizens cannot excuse themselves from public judgement — and it is there that he wrote the line coming closest to the famous saying. He is the nearest documented antecedent, not the author of the popular wording: Mill wrote that bad men need only that good men “look on and do nothing,” which is a different sentence from the one the internet quotes.

misattribution.heading: Three names, none of them right
misattribution.intro: This may be the most-quoted sentence in English political speech and one of the least sourced. It has been hung on at least three names over the past century, and the evidence supports none of them as its author.

items.scope: The credit on virtually every poster, mug and speech
items.why: The attribution has no documentary basis. Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations gave it the appearance of one in 1968 by citing Burke’s letter to William Smith of 9 January 1795 — but the letter contains no such sentence, and after William Safire challenged the citation in The New York Times in 1980, Bartlett’s fifteenth edition acknowledged the quotation had not been located in Burke’s writings, per Quote Investigator ↗. Barry Popik reaches the same verdict independently: never traced in his writings ↗.

items.scope: The usual correction offered by people who know it isn’t Burke
items.why: Mill genuinely wrote something very like it — “Bad men need nothing more to compass their ends, than that good men should look on and do nothing” — on page 36 of his 1867 St Andrews address ↗, and Wikiquote calls the famous line probably a paraphrase of it ↗. But Quote Investigator ↗ is careful to say Mill’s expression is conceptually related and not close textually. Putting the popular wording in Mill’s mouth simply relocates the error.

items.scope: A rarer variant credit that circulates online
items.why: Wikiquote records the saying being attributed to Tocqueville as well ↗, filed under “Unsourced, unverified, or other best guesses.” No source in Tocqueville is ever supplied with it — it is the same reflex that produced the Burke credit, applied to a second famous name.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who wrote it. Quote Investigator ↗ raises the possibility that the Rev. Charles F. Aked coined an early version in 1916 and that Sir R. Murray Hyslop pinned it on Burke in 1920 because it sounded like him — but concludes plainly that “the record is too incomplete to make strong claims about who crafted the quote.”

context.heading: How a sentence with no author got a founding father
lead: The line is a workhorse: presidents, prosecutors, editorial writers and staffroom posters all reach for it, and nearly all of them hand the credit to Edmund Burke. The trouble is that no one has ever located it in Burke. What survives instead is a chain of near-misses stretching across a century and a half — Burke on bad men combining in 1770, Mill on good men looking on in 1867, an anonymous adage circulating in American newspapers by 1916 — none of them the sentence itself.

The credit hardened because two sources with real authority repeated it. Quote Investigator ↗ documents President John F. Kennedy quoting the modern wording to the Canadian Parliament on 17 May 1961 and naming Burke, and Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations printing it under Burke in its 1968 fourteenth edition with a citation precise enough to look settled: a letter to William Smith dated 9 January 1795. When someone finally checked the letter, the sentence was not in it.
context.detailsSummary: What Burke actually wrote about good men and bad
detailsBody: Burke’s genuine passage comes from Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents, a pamphlet against the influence of the Court on the House of Commons, first published 23 April 1770 ↗: “When bad men combine, the good must associate; else they will fall one by one, an unpitied sacrifice in a contemptible struggle.”

Read in context it is not a rebuke of bystanders at all — it is an argument for organised political parties, made by a man defending the idea that principled men should band together rather than operate as freelancers. The famous saying converts a case for collective politics into a case against personal passivity. That is a shift in meaning, not merely in wording, which is one reason the substitution is worth correcting.
context.pull: Bartlett’s gave the line a date and a recipient. The letter turned out not to contain it.
